title: Prosecutor v. Galić — terror against the civilian population
question: Does a sustained campaign of sniping and shelling directed at civilians in a besieged city, conducted with the primary purpose of spreading terror among the civilian population, constitute a violation of the laws or customs of war?
facts: Over a period of approximately 23 months, forces under the accused's command conducted sniping and shelling attacks against civilian areas of a besieged city. The attacks struck civilians going about daily activities — queuing for water, attending funerals, crossing intersections. The pattern was sustained rather than isolated, and included attacks with no identifiable military objective in the vicinity. The accused held effective command over the forces conducting the attacks and received regular reports on their activities.
holding: The Trial Chamber held that the attacks constituted the crime of terror against the civilian population, and that the prohibition of attacks whose primary purpose is to spread terror among civilians forms part of customary international law, drawing on Article 51(2) of Additional Protocol I. The accused was convicted on the basis of command responsibility and direct participation.
key_reasoning: Article 51(2) AP I prohibits acts whose primary purpose is to spread terror among the civilian population
The prohibition has customary status applicable in both international and non-international armed conflict
The sustained pattern of attacks, rather than any single incident, established the primary purpose of spreading terror
Effective command plus knowledge of the attacks established command responsibility
